the-five-remembrances.name: The five remembrances
the-five-remembrances.how: Each day, recollect slowly: I am subject to ageing; to illness; to death; I will be parted from all that is dear; I am the owner of my actions, and will inherit them. Let each one sink in before the next.
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

mindfulness-of-death-maranasati.name: Mindfulness of death (maranasati)
mindfulness-of-death-maranasati.how: At nightfall and daybreak, reflect that death could come tonight or today from many causes, and ask whether any unskilful quality is still unabandoned. Let the urgency feed effort, not fear.
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

recollecting-the-round.name: Recollecting the round
recollecting-the-round.how: Contemplate how long the round of birth and death has been, and how many losses it holds, until disenchantment with becoming arises. Then turn to the breath and rest.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

powa-an-introduction-to-transference-at-.name: Powa: an introduction to transference at death
powa-an-introduction-to-transference-at-.how: Read a traditional introduction before seeking instruction from a qualified teacher: refuge, visualising Amitabha above the crown, and training the mind's direction at death. It is taught with empowerment, not from a page.
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.
Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

preparing-for-the-bardo.name: Preparing for the bardo
preparing-for-the-bardo.how: Notice the small gaps of daily life (falling asleep, the pause between thoughts) as rehearsals for the great transition, and rest there as awareness.
preparing-for-the-bardo.sourceLabel: Lion's Roar: The Fine Art of Conscious Dying (Glenn Mullin)
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

steps.text: Notice the small gaps of daily life (falling asleep, the pause between thoughts) as rehearsals for the great transition, and rest there as awareness.

self-enquiry-who-dies.name: Self-enquiry: who dies?
self-enquiry-who-dies.how: When the thought of death comes, ask to whom it comes. Trace the 'I' back to its source instead of following the thought. Ramana's own awakening began by lying down and enacting his death.
self-enquiry-who-dies.sourceLabel: Who Am I? (Sri Ramanasramam, free PDF)
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

practising-dying-melete-thanatou.name: Practising dying (melete thanatou)
practising-dying-melete-thanatou.how: Socrates calls philosophy the practice of dying: loosening the soul's grip on the body's pleasures and fears, day by day. Read the Phaedo slowly as an exercise, not an argument.
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

powa-an-introduction.name: Powa: an introduction
powa-an-introduction.how: A traditional introduction to transference at death; practised with a qualified teacher.
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.
Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

analytic-meditation-on-the-stages-of-the.name: Analytic meditation on the stages of the path
analytic-meditation-on-the-stages-of-the.how: Pick one Lamrim topic, such as the preciousness of this human life or the certainty of death. Think it through step by step, using reasons and examples, until a felt conviction comes. Then rest single-pointedly on that conviction for a while. Alternate thinking and resting.
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

self-enquiry.name: Self-enquiry
self-enquiry.how: Whenever a thought arises, ask to whom it arises; the answer is 'to me'; then ask 'who am I?' and hold attention on the sense of I.

steps.text: Whenever a thought arises, ask to whom it arises; the answer is 'to me'; then ask 'who am I?' and hold attention on the sense of I.

contemplating-not-self.name: Contemplating not-self
contemplating-not-self.how: Take each aggregate in turn and ask: is it constant, is it easeful, is it fitting to regard it as me, mine, my self?

steps.text: Take each aggregate in turn and ask: is it constant, is it easeful, is it fitting to regard it as me, mine, my self?

shiva-process-self-inquiry.name: Shiva Process self-inquiry
shiva-process-self-inquiry.how: Bring to mind a situation that is troubling you. Describe what you feel in plain words, then ask "what is the deeper feeling under this?" and keep going, layer by layer, until something shifts and the contraction releases. Often done in pairs or with a guide.

what-am-i-don-t-know.name: "What am I? Don't know"
what-am-i-don-t-know.how: Ask "What am I?" deeply on the in-breath. On the out-breath, hold "Don't know..." as long as the breath lasts. Return to this don't-know mind in every activity, and keep clear about the next correct action. This is Seung Sahn's Kwan Um teaching.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

owner-of-my-actions.name: Owner of my actions
owner-of-my-actions.how: The fifth remembrance: I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions. Recollect it before acting and after.

steps.text: The fifth remembrance: I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions.

mindfulness-of-breathing.name: Mindfulness of breathing
mindfulness-of-breathing.how: Sit comfortably, know the in-breath and out-breath, then let the breath calm the whole body before turning to feelings and mind.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

steps.text: Sit comfortably, know the in-breath and out-breath, then let the breath calm the whole body before turning to feelings and mind.

goodwill-metta.name: Goodwill (metta)
goodwill-metta.how: Wish yourself well, then widen the wish to others, near and far, seen and unseen, without exception.

steps.text: Wish yourself well, then widen the wish to others, near and far, seen and unseen, without exception.

resting-in-the-gap-between-breaths-vijna.name: Resting in the gap between breaths (Vijñāna Bhairava dhāraṇā)
resting-in-the-gap-between-breaths-vijna.how: Sit comfortably and breathe naturally. Notice the instant where the in-breath turns into the out-breath, and the instant where the out-breath turns back. Do not hold the breath; simply let attention fall into each turning point and rest there for its brief duration. Over time, notice the open awareness that is present in the pause.
resting-in-the-gap-between-breaths-vijna.sourceLabel: Bettina Bäumer, Vijñāna Bhairava verses 24–27 (the breath dhāraṇās).
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

recognition-pratyabhijna-contemplation.name: Recognition (pratyabhijñā) contemplation
recognition-pratyabhijna-contemplation.how: Read one sūtra of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam slowly. Then look at present experience — a sound, a thought, a feeling — and ask whether anything appears outside awareness. Let the understanding "this too is a form of the one consciousness" settle as a felt recognition rather than an idea. Return to the text, then to experience, alternating.
recognition-pratyabhijna-contemplation.sourceLabel: Christopher Wallis on the twenty sūtras of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam.

drawing-the-sri-chakra-as-meditation.name: Drawing the Śrī Chakra as meditation
drawing-the-sri-chakra-as-meditation.how: Following a teacher's step-by-step construction, draw the Śrī Yantra slowly from the centre point (bindu) outward: the nine interlocking triangles, the lotus rings and the square gateways. Treat each stage as a contemplation of the goddess unfolding into the world, not as geometry homework.
drawing-the-sri-chakra-as-meditation.sourceLabel: Devipuram, "How to Draw Sri Chakra" parts 1–2.

basic-saiva-siddhanta-meditation.name: Basic Śaiva Siddhānta meditation
basic-saiva-siddhanta-meditation.how: Sit upright, regulate the breath to a slow even count, then draw awareness inward from the senses to the spine and to the inner light, holding a single point of focus. Hinduism Today's monastery teaches it as part of daily worship and study.
basic-saiva-siddhanta-meditation.sourceLabel: Bodhinatha Veylanswami, "How Do We Meditate? Part 1".
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

mantra-repetition-japa.name: Mantra repetition (japa)
mantra-repetition-japa.how: Choose a mantra received from your tradition, sit with a mala, and repeat it at an even pace, aloud, whispered or mentally. Let attention rest on the sound and its meaning; when the mind wanders, return to the next repetition.

steps.text: Choose a mantra received from your tradition, sit with a mala, and repeat it at an even pace, aloud, whispered or mentally.

anapanasati-breath-meditation-method-2.name: Ānāpānasati (breath meditation, "Method 2")
anapanasati-breath-meditation-method-2.tradLabel: Dhammayut forest line (Ajahn Mun → Maha Boowa / Ajaan Lee)
anapanasati-breath-meditation-method-2.how: Sit upright and notice the breath at whatever point it is clearest. Let it settle into a comfortable rhythm, then let that sense of ease spread through the whole body, using the breath energy as a home base for steady, alert attention.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

buddho-recollection.name: "Buddho" recollection
buddho-recollection.how: Silently repeat "bud-" on the in-breath and "-dho" on the out-breath to anchor the mind; when the mind is calm, drop the word and stay with the knowing itself. Used widely in the Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah lines.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

walking-meditation-jongrom.name: Walking meditation (jongrom)
walking-meditation-jongrom.tradLabel: Ajahn Chah line (Wat Nong Pah Pong)
walking-meditation-jongrom.how: Choose a straight path of 15–30 paces. Walk at a natural or slow pace, attention on the feet or the whole body; at each end, stop, turn, and re-collect before walking back.

steps.text: Choose a straight path of 15–30 paces.

mahasi-noting.name: Mahasi noting
mahasi-noting.how: Watch the rise and fall of the abdomen and give each event a soft mental label ("rising", "falling", "thinking", "hearing"), then return to the primary object; move to slow walking with labels for lifting, moving and placing.

steps.text: Watch the rise and fall of the abdomen and give each event a soft mental label ("rising", "falling", "thinking", "hearing"), then return to the primary object; move to slow walking with labels for lifting, moving and placing.

natural-awareness-right-attitude.name: Natural awareness (right attitude)
natural-awareness-right-attitude.how: Instead of forcing focus on one object, relax and know whatever is being experienced, checking the attitude of the observing mind (craving, aversion, impatience) throughout daily activities.

steps.text: Instead of forcing focus on one object, relax and know whatever is being experienced, checking the attitude of the observing mind (craving, aversion, impatience) throughout daily activities.

satipatthana-four-establishings-of-mindf.name: Satipaṭṭhāna (four establishings of mindfulness)
satipatthana-four-establishings-of-mindf.how: Contemplate body, feeling, mind and mental qualities as they arise and pass, ardent, clearly knowing and mindful, without greed or distress about the world (MN 10).

steps.text: Contemplate body, feeling, mind and mental qualities as they arise and pass, ardent, clearly knowing and mindful, without greed or distress about the world (MN 10).

rain.name: RAIN
rain.how: Recognise what is happening; Allow it to be there; Investigate with kindness how it feels in the body; Nurture with self-compassion; then rest in the awareness that remains.

steps.text: Recognise what is happening; Allow it to be there; Investigate with kindness how it feels in the body; Nurture with self-compassion; then rest in the awareness that remains.

open-awareness-shamatha-without-a-suppor.name: Open awareness (shamatha without a support)
open-awareness-shamatha-without-a-suppor.how: After a few minutes with a support, let it go. Leave the eyes open and the gaze soft. Let sights, sounds and thoughts come and go, and do not follow them or push them away. When you get caught up, simply notice it and relax again. The point is to rest as the knowing that is already present.

looking-at-the-mind-mahamudra.name: Looking at the mind (Mahamudra)
looking-at-the-mind-mahamudra.how: Once the mind is calm, turn and look for the one who is looking. Ask where a thought comes from, where it stays, and where it goes. Do not reason about it; just look and rest in whatever is seen or not found. This practice is traditionally done under a qualified teacher's guidance.

resting-in-rigpa-dzogchen-orientation-on.name: Resting in rigpa (Dzogchen), orientation only
resting-in-rigpa-dzogchen-orientation-on.how: In Dzogchen, the student is introduced to the nature of mind (rigpa) by a teacher. Between sessions, practitioners recall that recognition, leave it uncontrived for short moments, many times, and release any effort to improve it. This entry describes the practice and is not a substitute for the introduction itself.
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.

shikantaza-just-sitting.name: Shikantaza (just sitting)
shikantaza-just-sitting.how: Sit as in zazen, but drop counting and any object. Simply sit, aware of the whole posture and the whole field of experience, without chasing or suppressing anything. When you find yourself lost in thought, come back to the posture. Dogen treats the sitting itself as realisation, not as a means to it.

koan-practice-with-mu.name: Koan practice with Mu
koan-practice-with-mu.how: Take up "Does a dog have buddha nature? Mu" (Zhaozhou). Breathe Mu on each exhalation and put your whole doubt into it. Do not interpret it. Present your understanding to a teacher in private interview (dokusan). Koan work depends on that meeting with a teacher.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

silent-illumination-mozhao.name: Silent illumination (mozhao)
silent-illumination-mozhao.how: Relax the body and be aware of the whole body sitting. Widen that awareness to include the environment, without any centre or edge. Silence means not adding commentary; illumination means remaining clearly aware. Rest there, and return whenever you get caught.

bhairavi-sadhana-isha.name: Bhairavi Sadhana (Isha)
bhairavi-sadhana-isha.how: A lay devotional observance offered by the Isha Foundation around Linga Bhairavi: for a set period the practitioner keeps simple disciplines (as given by Isha), offers daily devotion to the goddess, and completes it with an offering at a Linga Bhairavi abode. The exact rules come from the organisation each year.
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.

sravanamanananididhyasana.name: Śravaṇa–manana–nididhyāsana
sravanamanananididhyasana.how: Systematic listening to the Upaniṣads with a teacher (śravaṇa), resolving doubts by reflection (manana), and dwelling on the understood meaning until it is assimilated (nididhyāsana).

steps.text: Systematic listening to the Upaniṣads with a teacher (śravaṇa), resolving doubts by reflection (manana), and dwelling on the understood meaning until it is assimilated (nididhyāsana).

japa-repetition-of-a-divine-name.name: Japa (repetition of a divine name)
japa-repetition-of-a-divine-name.how: Repeat a mantra or name of God given by the teacher, often with a mālā of 108 beads, letting the mind rest in its meaning and the feeling of devotion.

steps.text: Repeat a mantra or name of God given by the teacher, often with a mālā of 108 beads, letting the mind rest in its meaning and the feeling of devotion.

hare-krishna-mahamantra-japa-and-kirtan.name: Hare Krishna mahāmantra (japa and kīrtan)
hare-krishna-mahamantra-japa-and-kirtan.how: Chant "Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare / Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare" softly on beads (japa) or sing it together (kīrtan), as practised since Chaitanya.

nembutsu-nianfo.name: Nembutsu / nianfo
nembutsu-nianfo.how: Recite "Namu Amida Butsu" (Japanese) or "Namo Amituofo" (Chinese), aloud or silently, with a mala if you like. In Chinese Pure Land, recitation is a practice of concentration and aspiration for rebirth. In Shin Buddhism, it is an expression of gratitude for Amida's vow, not a means of earning anything.

christian-meditation-with-a-mantra-maran.name: Christian meditation with a mantra (Maranatha)
christian-meditation-with-a-mantra-maran.how: Sit still and upright with your eyes lightly closed. Silently repeat one prayer-word, "Ma-ra-na-tha", in four equal syllables, listening to it rather than thinking about its meaning. When thoughts or images arrive, return to the word, without force. Sit for 20–30 minutes, morning and evening.

centering-prayer.name: Centering Prayer
centering-prayer.how: Choose a sacred word as a sign of consent to God's presence. Sit comfortably and bring it in gently. When you notice you are engaged with a thought, return ever so gently to the word. End by resting in silence for a couple of minutes. Twice daily, 20 minutes.

lectio-divina.name: Lectio Divina
lectio-divina.how: Read a short scripture passage slowly, then again; notice the word that catches you; respond to it in prayer; rest in silence. Read, ponder, pray, rest.

steps.text: Read a short scripture passage slowly, then again; notice the word that catches you; respond to it in prayer; rest in silence.

the-jesus-prayer-prayer-of-the-heart.name: The Jesus Prayer (prayer of the heart)
the-jesus-prayer-prayer-of-the-heart.how: Repeat "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me" slowly and attentively, often with a prayer rope, keeping the mind in the words and letting it descend into the heart. Begin with a fixed time each day; humility and stillness come before technique.

steps.text: Repeat "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me" slowly and attentively, often with a prayer rope, keeping the mind in the words and letting it descend into the heart.

zikr-remembrance-in-the-inayati-way.name: Zikr (remembrance) in the Inayati way
zikr-remembrance-in-the-inayati-way.how: Sitting quietly, repeat the phrase of divine unity (La ilaha illa'llah) aloud or silently, letting the breath and a gentle movement of the head carry it, until the remembrance continues on its own in the heart.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

steps.text: Sitting quietly, repeat the phrase of divine unity (La ilaha illa'llah) aloud or silently, letting the breath and a gentle movement of the head carry it, until the remembrance continues on its own in the heart.

dhikr-and-breathwork.name: Dhikr and breathwork
dhikr-and-breathwork.how: Join a short divine name or phrase to the in- and out-breath; keep attention on the heart; finish with silence and a prayer.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

steps.text: Join a short divine name or phrase to the in- and out-breath; keep attention on the heart; finish with silence and a prayer.

khatm-i-khwajagan-naqshbandi-group-dhikr.name: Khatm-i Khwajagan (Naqshbandi group dhikr)
khatm-i-khwajagan-naqshbandi-group-dhikr.how: A set Naqshbandi litany of Qur'an recitation, blessings on the Prophet and silent or vocal remembrance, recited together under a shaykh's guidance.

steps.text: A set Naqshbandi litany of Qur'an recitation, blessings on the Prophet and silent or vocal remembrance, recited together under a shaykh's guidance.

weekly-parashah-reflection-neo-hasidic.name: Weekly parashah reflection (neo-Hasidic)
weekly-parashah-reflection-neo-hasidic.how: Each week read the Torah portion with a Hasidic commentary in mind and look for the inward, devotional teaching it holds for this week of your life.

steps.text: Each week read the Torah portion with a Hasidic commentary in mind and look for the inward, devotional teaching it holds for this week of your life.

calming-and-contemplation-zhiguan.name: Calming and contemplation (zhiguan)
calming-and-contemplation-zhiguan.how: First calm the mind (zhi) by settling the breath and posture. Then contemplate (guan) any present thought as simultaneously empty, provisionally existing, and the middle, which are the threefold truth. Zhiyi's Mohe zhiguan sets out four kinds of samadhi practice (constant sitting, constant walking, half-walking half-sitting, and neither).
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

rudi-s-double-breath.name: Rudi's double breath
rudi-s-double-breath.how: Breathe in, bringing attention down from the throat into the heart, and then down to the navel and the base of the body. Breathing out, let the energy rise up the spine. Keep the movement gentle and continuous, and return to the heart when attention scatters.
rudi-s-double-breath.sourceLabel: Swami Khecaranatha on Rudi's double breath.
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.

khecari-mudra-historical-description-onl.name: Khecarī mudrā (historical description only)
khecari-mudra-historical-description-onl.how: Described in haṭha texts as turning the tongue back and up into the cavity above the soft palate, sometimes after gradually lengthening the tongue. We list it for context: the full form involves cutting the frenum and is not something to try from a video.
khecari-mudra-historical-description-onl.sourceLabel: Mallinson, The Khecarīvidyā (DPhil); no short clip on file.
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.

dream-yoga-first-steps.name: Dream yoga, first steps
dream-yoga-first-steps.how: During the day, keep reminding yourself "this is a dream" so that the habit carries into sleep. Before sleep, set a strong intention to recognise dreams. Visualise a luminous syllable at the throat as you fall asleep. Each morning, review whether you recognised a dream, and renew the intention.

feeding-your-demons-a-modern-adaptation-.name: Feeding your demons (a modern adaptation of Chöd)
feeding-your-demons-a-modern-adaptation-.how: Find a struggle, such as fear or a craving, and feel where it lives in the body. Picture it as a figure in front of you and ask what it wants and what it really needs. Then imagine dissolving your body into nectar that gives it exactly that, until it is satisfied. Rest in the open space that remains.

the-view-from-above-spiritual-exercise.name: The view from above (spiritual exercise)
the-view-from-above-spiritual-exercise.how: In imagination, rise above your situation until your concerns appear in the scale of the cosmos; return with a lighter, more just sense of what matters. One of the ancient "spiritual exercises" Pierre Hadot described.

steps.text: In imagination, rise above your situation until your concerns appear in the scale of the cosmos; return with a lighter, more just sense of what matters.

hermetic-ascent-and-rebirth-corpus-herme.name: Hermetic ascent and rebirth (Corpus Hermeticum XIII)
hermetic-ascent-and-rebirth-corpus-herme.how: Read slowly and as contemplation, not just as information: the treatise guides the reader to put away the "torments" of matter and be reborn as the intellect praising God in silence.

steps.text: Read slowly and as contemplation, not just as information: the treatise guides the reader to put away the "torments" of matter and be reborn as the intellect praising God in silence.

active-imagination-imaginal-attention.name: Active imagination / imaginal attention
active-imagination-imaginal-attention.how: Stay with an image (from a dream, a text or a place) as a living presence; let it speak and move; respond to it honestly rather than interpreting it away. In Corbin's terms it is a perception of the mundus imaginalis.

neelakantha-meditation.name: Neelakantha Meditation (mantra-based)
neelakantha-meditation.how: This is an initiated mantra practice: the mantra is received from an authorised teacher. In outline, one sits twice a day, repeats the given mantra inwardly and lets it become subtle, treating the body as a stable platform rather than an obstacle. Learn it from the school; we describe it only so users know what the clips refer to.

nyasa.name: Nyāsa — placing mantra on the body
nyasa.how: Touch or attend to specific points of the body (heart, head, crown, arms) while silently repeating the syllables assigned to them, so the body is treated as a seat of the deity before worship or meditation. Traditionally learnt with the specific mantra from a teacher.
nyasa.sourceLabel: Sthaneshwar Timalsina, "What is Nyasa and why do we do it?"

twelve-kalis.name: Contemplating the Twelve Kālīs (Krama)
twelve-kalis.how: Take one Kālī of the Krama sequence at a time (e.g. Sṛṣṭikālī, the Kālī of creation). Study what phase of cognition she stands for — an object arising, being held, being withdrawn into the knower — and watch that phase in your own experience during the day.

metta-loving-kindness.name: Mettā (loving-kindness)
metta-loving-kindness.how: Wish well to yourself, then a benefactor, a friend, a neutral person, a difficult person and finally all beings, using simple phrases or a felt sense of goodwill, letting it spread in every direction.

body-sweeping-goenka-vipassana.name: Body sweeping (Goenka vipassanā)
body-sweeping-goenka-vipassana.how: After a few days of ānāpāna to sharpen attention, move attention systematically through the body from head to feet, observing every sensation with equanimity, as taught in ten-day residential courses.

yoga-nidra.name: Yoga nidrā
yoga-nidra.how: Lying down, rotate awareness through the body, then breath, opposite sensations and visualisations while staying awake, ending with a personal resolve (saṅkalpa).
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

five-points-of-yoga-sivananda.name: Five points of yoga (Sivananda)
five-points-of-yoga-sivananda.how: Proper exercise (āsana), proper breathing (prāṇāyāma), proper relaxation, proper diet and positive thinking with meditation, as summarised by Swami Vishnudevananda.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

breath-centred-individually-adapted-asan.name: Breath-centred, individually adapted āsana (viniyoga)
breath-centred-individually-adapted-asan.how: Link every movement to a slow inhale or exhale and adapt sequence, length and intensity to the person's body, age and aims, as taught by Krishnamacharya and T. K. V. Desikachar.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

shamatha-with-object.name: Calm abiding with a support
shamatha-with-object.how: Sit upright and relaxed. Rest your attention lightly on a simple support, such as the breath at the nostrils, a pebble, or a sound. When you notice the mind has wandered, return to the support without scolding yourself. Aim for many short, clear sessions rather than a few long, dull ones. Over time, loosen your grip until attention rests on its own.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

tonglen.name: Tonglen (sending and taking)
tonglen.how: Flash briefly on open, spacious mind. Then breathe in a feeling of heaviness and heat, and breathe out a feeling of coolness and light. Start with a real person who is suffering, perhaps yourself, and breathe in their pain while breathing out relief. Widen this to everyone who feels the same. Keep it simple and close to how you actually feel.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

lojong-slogans.name: Mind training (lojong) slogans
lojong-slogans.how: Choose one of the 59 slogans of Atisha's Seven Points, such as "Drive all blames into one". Carry it through the day. When irritation or self-cherishing comes up, recall the slogan and look again at the situation. Review the day each evening.

nine-breathings.name: Nine breathings of purification
nine-breathings.how: Visualise the three channels: a central blue channel with a white one on the right and a red one on the left. Breathe in through the right nostril and out through the left three times, releasing anger. Then breathe in through the left and out through the right three times, releasing attachment. Finally, breathe in through both and push the breath up the central channel three times, releasing ignorance. Rest afterwards.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

zazen.name: Zazen posture and breath
zazen.how: Sit on a cushion with your knees on the floor, or on a chair, with the spine upright. Rest the hands in the cosmic mudra, left on right with the thumbs lightly touching, and keep the eyes half-open and lowered. Breathe naturally through the nose. Beginners can count breaths from one to ten and start again whenever they lose count.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

huatou.name: Huatou (critical phrase)
huatou.how: Take up a short question, such as "What is wu?" or "Before my parents were born, what was my original face?" Keep asking it with a sense of genuine not-knowing until a "great doubt" gathers. Return to the question whenever you lose it. This is Sheng Yen's method, best done in retreat with guidance.

mindful-breathing-pv.name: Mindful breathing with gathas
mindful-breathing-pv.how: Breathe in and silently say "In"; breathe out and say "Out". As you settle, shorten it to "Deep / Slow", "Calm / Ease" or "Smile / Release". Use a bell or a phone chime as a reminder to stop, breathe three times and come back to the body.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

walking-meditation.name: Walking meditation
walking-meditation.how: Walk slowly and coordinate your steps with your breath, for example two steps on the in-breath and three on the out-breath. Feel each foot touching the earth as if kissing it. You are not trying to arrive anywhere; every step is the arrival.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

ajikan.name: Ajikan (A-syllable meditation)
ajikan.how: Shingon practitioners visualise the Sanskrit syllable A on a moon disc above a lotus. The A signifies the unborn source of all things. They join it with the breath and expand the moon until it fills the universe, then contract it into the heart. Formal ajikan is taught after initiation; this entry is an orientation only.
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.

video-lectio.name: Video lectio (short contemplative reading)
video-lectio.how: Watch a short image or text slowly, then sit with a single phrase that stays with you before meditating.

welcoming-practice.name: Welcoming Practice
welcoming-practice.how: When a strong reaction arises, feel it as a sensation in the body; say "welcome" to it instead of resisting; then let go of the desire for security, approval or control, and so release it into presence.

neoplatonic-contemplation.name: Neoplatonic contemplation ("strip away everything")
neoplatonic-contemplation.how: Following Plotinus, turn attention from objects to the activity of knowing, then let even that subtle self-image fall away, resting in the simple presence it comes from. Usually practised after a period of calming meditation.

unio-mystica-letters.name: Letter-combination meditation (ecstatic Kabbalah)
unio-mystica-letters.how: Abulafia's path: combine and permute the Hebrew letters of divine names, with breath and pronunciation, to loosen ordinary thinking. Historically taught only under a teacher. Listed here for context, not as instruction.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

middle-pillar-outline.name: The Middle Pillar (outline)
middle-pillar-outline.tradLabel: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
middle-pillar-outline.how: Stand or sit straight. Picture a slender pillar of light along the midline of the body. Bring attention to five centers in turn, seeing each as a sphere of its colour: brilliant white above the crown; soft lavender at the throat; rose pink at the heart; deep violet at the loins; and at the feet the four earth tones quartered. Dwell briefly at each. Then picture light circulating: down the front of the body and up the spine, around and around, steady with the breath. Close by letting the light settle and fade. Learn the full form from the order or a qualified teacher; this outline only shows what the exercise is.
middle-pillar-outline.sourceLabel: Regardie, The Middle Pillar (1938). Centres, colours and circulation as published; vibratory formulae omitted. Wikipedia link checked 200 on 2026-10-20.
cautions: Energy visualisation: stop if you feel agitated, pressured in the head or chest, or unwell.

ease-through-the-body-trika-prep.name: Ease through the body with the breath (Trika prep)
ease-through-the-body-trika-prep.how: Sit upright and let the breath settle into a comfortable rhythm. Notice where the breath is clearest and rest attention there. Let that sense of ease spread through the whole body, using the breath as a home base for steady attention. When the mind wanders, return gently to the breath without force. Close by sitting quietly for a few breaths and noticing the whole body at once.
ease-through-the-body-trika-prep.sourceLabel: Thanissaro Bhikkhu breath method (free, publisher site); used here as the Trika-prep foundation for steady attention before gap and recognition work.
cautions: Keep the breath natural; never hold it or force it.
If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.

vbt-sound-dissolution.name: Listening to the inner sound (VBT verses 38-39)
vbt-sound-dissolution.how: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle by itself. Listen for a faint inner sound, a soft ringing or hum beneath the sounds of the room. Rest attention on it lightly, without straining to hear. Let it be loud, soft, present or absent; do not follow it into images or stories. When the mind wanders, come back to listening. If the sound fades into quiet, rest in the quiet. When you finish, notice the ordinary sounds around you again.

cautions: If you live with tinnitus that distresses you, listen instead to an outer sound such as a bell or a held note as it fades (verses 40-41).

vbt-body-as-consciousness.name: The body as awareness (VBT verse 63)
vbt-body-as-consciousness.how: Sit and let attention rest on the whole body at once: not one part, the whole field of sensation. Then take the body, and the world around it, as made of awareness. Let this be felt rather than thought. When the mind narrows back to "me" and "mine", return to the wider field and rest there. The body stays where it is; only the sense of it being separate softens.
vbt-body-as-consciousness.sourceLabel: Vijñāna Bhairava verse 63, tr. Christopher Hareesh Wallis (Tantra 112 full text). Satsang summary in its own words.
cautions: If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.

The rest of the Vijñāna Bhairava (breath retention, mantra, the subtle-body and burning practices) is learned from a qualified teacher in the Trika tradition; Satsang lists places to practise.

vbt-mind-between-objects.name: Resting between objects (VBT verse 62)
vbt-mind-between-objects.how: First settle with the breath for a few minutes. Then notice the moment the mind lets go of one thing, a sensation, a thought, a sound, and before it takes up the next. Rest in that in-between. Do not chase the next object and do not push it away. When you find you have already moved on, come back to the gap. Practise the breath-pause sit first; this one needs a little steadiness.

vbt-space-contemplation.name: Spaciousness: a wall of skin with nothing inside (VBT verses 43-48)
vbt-space-contemplation.how: Sit and notice the space of the room around you, the space that holds the walls and your body. Then sense the space inside the body: the chest, the mouth, the skull. Feel the skin as a thin wall with open space within and without. Let the inner and outer space be one field and rest in that openness. When the mind reaches for something solid, notice the reaching and return to space. Stay alert; this is not a blank or sleepy state.

vbt-twelve-centres.name: Touching the end-of-twelve through the day (VBT verse 51)
vbt-twelve-centres.how: This is a daily-life practice, not a sit. Several times a day, while walking, waiting or eating, let attention rest for a few breaths at the space just above the crown of the head, the "end of twelve", then carry on with what you were doing. Keep the touch light and brief. The remembering is the practice.

cautions: If attention above the head brings headache, pressure or dizziness, rest it in the heart or the soles of the feet instead.

vbt-inner-outer-spaces.name: Merging the sense spaces (VBT verses 32-33)
vbt-inner-outer-spaces.how: Sit and bring attention to one sense contact: a sound, a touch, something seen. Notice the outer space where it arrives, the room and the distance. Then notice the inner space where it is received. Rest in both at once, the outer and the inner as one field with the sensation in the middle. When attention falls to one side, come back to both.

theme-verse-reflection.name: Theme verse reflection (upasamanussati)
theme-verse-reflection.how: Sit. Recite the theme verse slowly, in Pali then English: stilling of preparations, relinquishment of assets, destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, extinction. Rest attention on each phrase for three breaths. Do not analyse. Let each phrase land. When the mind argues, return to the next phrase. Ten minutes.

cautions: If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.

wound-location.name: Locating the wound (craving in the body)
wound-location.how: Sit. When craving arises for anything, do not follow it to its object. Instead ask: where in the body is this felt? Chest? Throat? Belly? Rest attention on the location, not the story. The location is the wound. The story is the arrow's feathers. Ten minutes, or until the craving shifts.
wound-location.sourceLabel: Sermon 1 wound-and-surgeon simile (acchecchi tanham idha namarupe). The bandage goes on the wound. From Ven. Kaṭukurunde Ñāṇananda, Nibbāna: The Mind Stilled (free at seeingthroughthenet.net). Satsang summary in its own words.
cautions: If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.
If you have a history of trauma, dissociation, psychosis or severe anxiety, keep sits short with eyes open, or practise with a qualified teacher or clinician.

fire-contemplation.name: Fire going out (extinction contemplation)
fire-contemplation.how: Light a candle, or picture one. Watch the flame. It burns because of fuel and air meeting. Now imagine the fuel running out — not blown out, just exhausted. The flame doesn't go anywhere. It stops happening. Sit with that image for ten minutes. Then close the eyes and feel the body's own little fires: hunger, wanting, restlessness. Same mechanism.
fire-contemplation.sourceLabel: Sermon 1 fire simile (Aggivacchagotta). Wood burns because of fire, fire because of wood — this-to-that relatedness. From Ven. Kaṭukurunde Ñāṇananda, Nibbāna: The Mind Stilled (free at seeingthroughthenet.net). Satsang summary in its own words.
cautions: Never leave a lit candle unattended; picturing the flame works as well.

root-pattern-seeing.name: Seeing the root pattern (mula-pariyaya)
root-pattern-seeing.how: Pick one sense door — hearing is easiest. For five minutes, notice each sound and the instant 'I' gets added: 'I hear it,' 'I like it,' 'I want it to stop.' Just notice the adding. Don't stop it. The noticing IS the practice. The 'I' is a postscript, not the text.
root-pattern-seeing.sourceLabel: Sermon 13 mula-pariyaya. Conceiving earth as earth, delighting, 'I am earth' — the full proliferation in one sutta. From Ven. Kaṭukurunde Ñāṇananda, Nibbāna: The Mind Stilled (free at seeingthroughthenet.net). Satsang summary in its own words.
cautions: If you feel disoriented, unreal or anxious, open the eyes, feel the feet and the seat, and stop for today.

bahiya-practice.name: Only the seen (Bahiya instruction)
bahiya-practice.how: Choose one sense — sight is clearest. For ten minutes: in the seen, only the seen. When 'I see it' arises, drop the 'I', keep the seeing. When commentary starts, drop it, keep the colours and shapes. This is not suppression — it is subtraction. The seeing was always just seeing.
bahiya-practice.sourceLabel: Sermon 15 Bahiya instruction. No experiencer added to experience. From Ven. Kaṭukurunde Ñāṇananda, Nibbāna: The Mind Stilled (free at seeingthroughthenet.net). Satsang summary in its own words.

observer-inquiry.name: Looking for the observer
observer-inquiry.how: Sit in signless rest. Then ask, gently: who is resting? Who is aware? Look for the looker. Do not answer with philosophy — look. If you find tension, a watcher-feeling, a subtle 'me' holding the sit together — notice it as one more sign. Let it be there without serving it. Ten minutes. The looking is the practice; there is no finding.
observer-inquiry.sourceLabel: Sermons 16-17. The observer is the last sign. Seeing through it is the last gate. From Ven. Kaṭukurunde Ñāṇananda, Nibbāna: The Mind Stilled (free at seeingthroughthenet.net). Satsang summary in its own words.

collections.title: Seven days with death
collections.intro: One short talk and one practice a day for a week. The traditions agree on little, but they agree that remembering death changes how we live. Go gently; skip a day whenever you need to.
collections.author: Satsang

units.title: The one certainty
units.intro: Start with the plain fact: everyone who is born dies.

items.note: What would I stop putting off if I took this seriously?

units.title: Mindfulness of death
units.intro: The Buddha asked monks to recall death with every breath.

units.title: Who dies?
units.intro: Advaita turns the question around: find who it is that is afraid.

units.title: The moment of death and after
units.intro: Tibetan teachers map the dying process and the bardo in detail.

items.note: Preparing for the bardo, a short orientation on the Rebirth hub.

units.title: Grief and loss
units.intro: Death is also what happens to the people we love.

units.title: Practising dying
units.intro: Plato called philosophy a rehearsal for death.

units.title: What remains
units.intro: End where the traditions point: the deathless, the Self, the open sky of mind.

items.note: What did this week change, if anything?

collections.title: Rebirth across traditions
collections.intro: Does anything carry on after death? One talk from each tradition that answers, then the classic texts to read for free.

units.intro: Theravada: actions have consequences that outlive this body. Start with the five remembrances.
units.title: The owner of my actions

items.note: Which of the five lands hardest? That one is your teacher this week.

units.intro: Tibetan: between death and rebirth lies the bardo. Prepare for it the way you would for a journey.
units.title: The between-state

items.note: What would you pack for a journey you cannot refuse?

units.intro: Advaita: before asking what is reborn, find who it is that fears death.
units.title: Who dies?

items.note: Notice the difference between thinking about the seeker and looking for it.

units.intro: Early suttas and the Platonists both kept death in daily view. Recollect the round; practise dying.
units.title: Remembering, both ways

items.note: Two traditions, one exercise: what changes when death is remembered daily?

units.intro: Close with the shared ground: mindfulness of death as urgency for practice, not fear.
units.title: Urgency, not fear

items.note: What would you stop putting off if you took impermanence seriously?
Nineteen free essays and texts on the Rebirth hub, from the suttas to the Myth of Er.

collections.title: Kashmir Shaivism: a first syllabus
collections.intro: The nondual Śaiva tradition of Kashmir, in six steps: a theory track of short talks from scholars and teachers, and a practice track of simple contemplations from the Vijñāna Bhairava and the Pratyabhijñā.

collections.title: Thai Forest: the basics
collections.intro: The forest tradition of Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah, as its Western monks teach it today: virtue, the breath, Buddho, walking, and how to bring it into a life.

collections.title: Visualisations: the Tibetan deity practice primer
collections.intro: Orientation only. Deity yoga is taught in Tibetan Buddhism after an empowerment and with a teacher; this primer explains what it is and why it is practised, through talks by teachers of the tradition. It does not teach the visualisations themselves.

collections.title: Metta in four traditions
collections.intro: Goodwill, loving-kindness, compassion: four ways of growing a kind heart, one sit at a time.

collections.author: Wiser
collections.intro: One outline, seven sittings. Each day adds one centre to the pillar, then rests in the circulation. Ten minutes a day. This is orientation only: the full form is learnt in the order or from a qualified teacher.
collections.title: Middle Pillar week

units.intro: The pillar first: light along the midline, crown to feet. Nothing else.
units.title: The pillar

items.note: Can you feel the midline as one continuous line? If not, that is the work.

units.intro: Add the crown: brilliant white above the head, the source of the light.
units.title: Crown

items.note: White first: the colour of undifferentiated light.

units.intro: Add the throat: soft lavender, where the light narrows into speech.
units.title: Throat

items.note: Notice any pressure in the throat and breathe around it, never through force.

units.intro: Add the heart: rose pink, the largest sphere, the seat of the circulation.
units.title: Heart

items.note: The heart centre carries the practice. Give it the most time.

units.intro: Add the loins: deep violet, where the light gathers before descending.
units.title: Loins

items.note: Gathering is not grasping. Let the violet hold without pulling.

units.intro: Add the feet: the quartered earth tones grounding the whole pillar.
units.title: Feet

items.note: A pillar with no foundation is a fantasy. Feel the feet.

units.intro: The whole week in one sit: five centres, then the circulation down the front and up the spine with the breath.
units.title: The circulation

items.note: If the circuit runs on its own, let it. If not, return to the heart.

collections.title: Trika prep week
collections.author: Wiser
collections.intro: Seven days of foundation for Abhinavagupta and VBT study: steady breath, the turn of the breath, and recognition. Ten minutes a day. Initiated practices are not here: when the gap is steady, take the next step with a qualified teacher in the tradition.

units.title: Settle
units.intro: The home base: ease through the body with the breath.

items.note: Where is the breath clearest today? That is your seat for the week.

units.title: The turn
units.intro: Notice where the in-breath becomes the out-breath. Rest there; hold nothing.

items.note: Did you find the turning, or the idea of it? Either is fine — noted, not judged.

units.title: Recognition
units.intro: One sutra slowly, then look: does anything appear outside awareness?

items.note: Write one sentence on what recognition felt like versus what you thought about it.

units.title: Return to ease
units.intro: Same foundation, deeper seat. The gap work needs a rested body.

items.note: Compare today with day 1: steadier, sleepier, brighter? Log it plainly.

units.title: Longer turn
units.intro: Same gap practice, full sit. Let attention fall in; never force it.

items.note: If strain appears, drop back to ease. The gap is found, not made.

units.title: Recognition again
units.intro: Same contemplation, fresh experience. Sound, thought, feeling — inside or outside?

items.note: One line for the journal: what was recognised, and by what?

units.title: The week in one sit
units.intro: Ease, then the turn, then recognition — one short sit chaining all three in order.

items.note: Which of the three is your door? That is what you take to a teacher next.

collections.title: VBT Foundations
collections.author: Wiser
collections.intro: Seven contemplative practices from the Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra, in a progression from the breath to daily life (not the text's own order): the turn of the breath, the gap between objects, inner sound, the body as awareness, the sense spaces, spaciousness, and the end-of-twelve through the day. Each is a quiet sit you can do on your own. The rest of the text (breath retention, mantra, the subtle-body practices) is learned from a qualified teacher: when one of these becomes your door, take it to a teacher in the tradition.

units.title: Breath-pause
units.intro: The first practice the text presents: resting in the gap between the in-breath and the out-breath.

items.note: Did you find the turning, or the idea of it? Either is fine — noted, not judged.

units.title: The gap between thoughts
units.intro: When the mind lets go of one thing and before it takes up the next, rest in the middle. Build on day 1's steadiness.

items.note: How long was the gap today? One thought-width, or longer?

units.title: Inner sound
units.intro: Listen to the subtle inner sound until sound dissolves into silence.

items.note: What quality was the sound — ring, hum, tone, silence? Log it plainly.

units.title: Body as consciousness
units.intro: Conceive of the body — or the whole universe — as nothing but consciousness. A felt sense, not an idea.

items.note: Did the body-sense shift, or was it the same body with a different label? Both are data.

units.title: Inner and outer spaces
units.intro: A sense contact — the outer space where it arrives, the inner space where it is received, both as one field.

items.note: Which side did attention collapse into — inner or outer? That is the habit to notice.

units.title: Spaciousness
units.intro: The space of the room, the space inside the body, the skin as a thin wall between: one open field.

items.note: When did the mind grasp for something solid? What did it grasp at?

units.title: The end-of-twelve through the day
units.intro: Not a sitting practice. A few times today, let attention touch the space just above the crown for a breath or two, then carry on.

items.note: How many times today did you remember? The remembering is the practice, not the count.
